p.src: Meanwhile, the rebel Wang Qing deployed his troops to meet the enemy. Apart from Wenren Shichong and the other naval officers, who had already received their assignments, he appointed Liu Yijing, the false Military Supervisor of Yun’an Prefecture, as chief vanguard, and Shangguan Yi, the false Military Supervisor of Dongchuan, as deputy vanguard. Li Xiong and Bi Xian, false commanders of Nanfeng, formed the left wing; Liu Yuan and Pan Zhong, false commanders of Ande, formed the right wing; the false senior commander Duan Wu commanded the main rear guard, with Qiu Xiang, the false Commissioner of the Imperial Camp, as his deputy; and the false Privy Councillor Fang Han supported the central army. Wang Qing himself commanded the central army, attended by many false ministers, imperial-camp guards, generals of the royal escort, commandants, and several dozen subordinate officers serving under them. Li Zhu served as marshal. The ranks of men and horses were perfectly ordered, and Wang Qing supervised them in person. The horses wore leather armor and the men iron mail; bows and crossbows were strung, and at three rolls of the war drums the entire army moved out. They had gone less than ten li when, where dust rose ahead, scouts of the Song army could already be seen approaching. Amid the chiming of horse bells came some thirty mounted scouts. All wore blue warriors’ kerchiefs and green battle robes; their horses bore red tassels, dozens of bronze bells hung on either side, and a spray of pheasant feathers rose behind. They carried slender silver-ringed long spears, light bows, and short arrows. The warrior at their head was Zhang Qing, the Featherless Arrow, Cavalry General of the Tigers, restored to his former office by imperial command of Emperor Daojun. On his head was a blue kerchief embroidered in gold; he wore an embroidered green battle robe, a purple silken sash at his waist, and soft fragrant-leather boots, and rode a horse with a silver saddle. To his left rode Qiongying, the Jade Arrowhead, imperially titled Lady of Chastity and Filial Devotion. She wore a purple-gold phoenix coronet set with pearls, an embroidered purple gauze battle robe, a multicolored silken sash, and vermilion embroidered shoes with tiny phoenix-shaped toes, and sat a fine silver-maned horse. A little behind on the right, bearing the banner, rode Ye Qing, imperially appointed Loyal Servant and Senior Rank-and-File Officer. They scouted straight up to Li Zhu’s army and, when no more than a hundred paces away, reined about and returned. Liu Yijing and Shangguan Yi, the vanguards of the front army, spurred their horses, drove their troops forward, and charged. Zhang Qing urged on his horse, leveled his white pear-blossom spear, and engaged the two generals. Qiongying galloped forward with her painted square-bladed halberd leveled and joined the fight. After the four had fought for more than ten bouts, Zhang Qing and Qiongying knocked aside the rebel generals’ weapons, wheeled their horses, and retreated. Liu Yijing and Shangguan Yi drove their troops in pursuit, but men on either side shouted, “Vanguards, do not chase them! The brocade bags behind their saddles are full of stones, and they never miss a man!” Only on hearing this did Liu Yijing and Shangguan Yi rein in their horses. Then the drums thundered behind Longmen Mountain, and five hundred infantrymen came wheeling into view. At their head came four infantry leaders: Li Kui, the Black Whirlwind; Fan Rui, the Demon King of Chaos; Xiang Chong, the Eight-Armed Nezha; and Li Gun, the Flying Great Sage. They rushed straight forward. The five hundred infantrymen formed a single line below the slope and planted their round shields firmly on both flanks. Liu Yijing and Shangguan Yi drove their troops forward in a sweeping attack; Li Kui and Fan Rui split the infantry into two columns, and all, carrying their barbarian shields reversed, rounded the slope and withdrew. By then Wang Qing and Li Zhu had arrived with the main army, and all charged forward together. Li Kui, Fan Rui, and the others raced up the mountain, crossed the ridge, plunged into the woods, and vanished from sight. Li Zhu gave orders for the troops and cavalry to form battle lines there on the broad, open plain. Suddenly a cannon sounded behind the mountain, and from the southern side a force came surging forth, clustered around three generals. In the center was Wang Ying, the Stumpy Tiger; on the left, Sun Xin, the Little Yuchi; and on the right, Zhang Qing, the Gardener. Commanding five thousand horse and foot, they came charging forward. Just as Wang Qing was about to send a general to meet them, another cannon boomed behind the mountain. From the northern side another force surged forth around three women generals.

p.src: In the center was Hu Sanniang, Ten Feet of Steel; on the left, Gu Dasao, the Tigress; and on the right, Sun Erniang, the Female Yaksha. Leading five thousand horse and foot, they charged forward and met the troops of Liu Yuan and Pan Zhong on the rebels’ right wing, engaging them in battle. Wang Ying and his companions met the troops of Li Xiong and Bi Xian on the rebels’ left wing, and battle was joined. After each side had fought for more than ten bouts, Wang Ying, Sun Xin, and Zhang Qing in the south reined their horses about and led their troops away to the east; in the north, Hu Sanniang, Gu Dasao, and Sun Erniang likewise wheeled their mounts and led their troops eastward. Watching them, Wang Qing laughed and said, “Song Jiang has nothing but these wretched men and women under him! How, then, have my officers and soldiers suffered defeat time after time?” He thereupon drove his great army forward in pursuit and attack. They had gone no more than five or six li when a sharp gong suddenly sounded. The four infantry leaders who had withdrawn before—Li Kui, Fan Rui, Xiang Chong, and Li Gun—came wheeling out of the woods to the left of the mountain. They had been joined by four more infantry officers: Lu Zhishen, the Tattooed Monk; Wu Song, the Pilgrim; Jiao Ting, the Faceless; and Liu Tang, the Red-Haired Demon. With five hundred infantrymen, all armed with round shields and short weapons, they charged straight forward. Shangguan Yi, deputy vanguard of the rebel army, hurriedly turned two thousand infantrymen against them. Li Kui and Lu Zhishen exchanged only a few bouts with the rebel troops before feigning that they could not withstand them. Carrying their round shields reversed, they split into two groups and fled swiftly into the woods. The rebel troops pursued, but Li Kui and the others were swift of foot, and in the snap of a finger they had scattered in every direction and vanished. Seeing this, Li Zhu hastily said to Wang Qing, “Your Majesty must not pursue them. This is a ruse to lure us in. Let us first form our ranks and meet the enemy.”

p.src: At the east gate stood Shi En, the Gold-Eyed Tiger; at the west gate, Zheng Tianshou, the Fair-Faced Gentleman; at the south gate, Song Wan, the Vajra in the Clouds; and at the north gate, Xue Yong, the Sick Tiger. Behind the yellow banners stood a mass of gun carriages. Ling Zhen, the Thunderbolt, commanded there as master gunner, surrounded by more than twenty assistants and the artillery. Behind the carriages were arrayed grappling hooks and lassos for capturing enemy commanders; beyond them rose a ring of many-colored standards, with the stars of the Twenty-Eight Mansions stationed on all four sides. Amid the gold-embroidered banners stood a goose-yellow command standard, embroidered in raised velvet, edged with pearls, hung with golden bells at its foot, and crowned with pheasant feathers. Guarding it was a mighty warrior whose cap bore a fishtail ornament and whose armor folded like dragon scales. Ten feet tall and awe-inspiring, he was Yu Baosi, the Perilous-Road God. Beside the banner were two mounted guards, identically equipped and each holding a steel spear: Kong Ming, the Hairy-Headed Star, and Kong Liang, the Lone Fire Star. Before and behind their horses stood twenty-four armored soldiers bearing wolf-toothed clubs. Behind them were two embroidered battle standards, and amid twenty-four halberds arrayed on either side stood two valiant commanders. On the left was Lü Fang, the Little Marquis Wen; on the right, Guo Sheng, the Rival of Rengui. Each held a decorated halberd and sat his horse on one side. Between the halberds stood a cluster of steel forks and two identically equipped infantry champions: Xie Zhen, the Double-Headed Serpent, and Xie Bao, the Double-Tailed Scorpion. Each wielded a three-pronged lotus fork and guarded the central army. Next, mounted on two horses with brocade saddles, were Xiao Rang, the Sacred-Handed Scholar, on the left, and Pei Xuan, the Iron-Faced Judge, on the right. Behind their horses stood men in purple bearing ceremonial tallies, together with soldiers armed with mazha sabers. Amid that forest of mazha sabers stood two executioners: in the higher place Cai Fu, the Iron Arm, and below him Cai Qing, the Flower. On both rear flanks were companies of gold- and silver-spear troops, each led by a great commander. The gold-spear company was commanded by Xu Ning, the Gold-Lanced Warrior. The silver-spear company was commanded by Hua Rong, the Lesser Li Guang. Behind them came pairs of men in brocade, pairs in flowered caps, clusters in scarlet robes, and throngs in brocade jackets. On both sides rose green canopies and emerald curtains, vermilion standards and parasols, yellow battle-axes and white yak-tail banners, and bright blades flashing blue. Between two ranks bearing axes, whips, and maces, beneath three gold-embroidered parasols, three heroes sat on fine horses with brocade saddles. On the right, wearing a starry crown and crane-feather robe, was Gongsun Sheng, the Dragon in the Clouds, who could summon wind and rain. On the left, wearing a silk cap and holding a feather fan, was Wu Yong, the Resourceful Star, accomplished in both civil and military arts. In the center, on the jade-white Night-Shining Lion with its golden saddle, sat the humane and righteous chief vanguard of the western expedition, who had repelled the invaders and pacified the rebels: Song Gongming of Shandong, the Timely Rain and Guardian of Righteousness. Fully accoutred and personally armed with his precious Kunwu sword, he supervised the battle from within the formation and commanded the central army. Before his horse on the left stood Dai Zong, the Marvelous Traveler, charged with carrying urgent military reports and directing troop deployments. On the right stood Yan Qing, the Prodigal, specially charged with guarding the central army and handling confidential affairs. Behind the horses, great halberds and long spears rose above fine mounts with brocade saddles. Thirty-five staff officers sat their warhorses in perfect order, each holding a long spear and carrying a full bow and quiver. Behind them, battle horns sounded and the full military band played in splendor. At the rear of the formation two more mobile detachments lay in ambush on either side as wings protecting the central army. p.src: Just then the war drums in the Song army began to thunder without cease. Wang Qing and Li Zhu descended from the command platform and mounted their warhorses. Officers of the imperial guard and other attendants protected them on either side, while many eunuchs crowded behind their horses. Wang Qing issued an imperial command ordering the vanguard to advance and attack. The two armies faced each other east and west, and the celestial stem and earthly branch of that day belonged to wood. When the gate banners opened on the due west side of the Song formation, Lin Chong, the Panther-Head, galloped out beneath them, and both armies raised a tremendous shout. Lin Chong reined in his horse, leveled his eighteen-foot serpent spear, and shouted sternly, “Ignorant traitors! Mad rebels plotting against the throne! The armies of Heaven have arrived, yet still you will not surrender! If you wait until flesh and bone are ground to mud, it will be too late for regret!” In the rebel formation, Li Zhu had once been a fortune-teller and thoroughly understood the principles of mutual generation and conquest among the elements. He hurriedly issued an order for Liu Yuan and Pan Zhong of the right wing to lead the red-banner troops in an attack. Liu Yuan and Pan Zhong obeyed, leading the red-banner troops forward at a gallop to attack. Shouts rose again and again from both formations as all the war drums thundered together. Lin Chong met Liu Yuan in combat; four arms swept back and forth, and eight hooves churned in confusion. Lin Chong's deputy commanders, Huang Xin and Sun Li, galloped out from the formation. Huang Xin swung his Gate-of-Mourning sword and hacked at Pan Zhong. A bloody forehead flashed, flesh still clinging to it, as the golden helmet fell beside the horse.

How the wolf-brush defeats the shield: if the shield-bearer rolls forward bodily, the brush counters with a sweeping gust; if the shield pursues from the flank, the brush awaits it with a diagonal thrust; if the shield presses and barges inward, the brush retreats and thrusts. How the shield counters the wolf-brush: if the brush comes level with the chest, the shield evades with the Little Crouch posture; if the brush closes in densely, the shield follows with the Shredding Shears technique. Single sabers swept, coiled, and twisted, feigning defeat and contriving retreat; iron forks barred above and covered below, advancing obliquely, bracing and dodging. p.src: Lu Junyi, Yang Xiong, and Shi Xiu fought their way into the central army and ran straight into Fang Han, whom Lu Junyi killed with a single spear thrust. They scattered the troops guarding the central command and went directly to seize Wang Qing, only to encounter “Master Golden Sword” Li Zhu. Li Zhu was skilled in sword magic, and his sword flashed through the air like lightning. Lu Junyi was finding himself unable to withstand him when Song Jiang’s central forces arrived. At their right was Gongsun Sheng, the “Dragon in the Clouds,” who muttered an incantation and shouted, “Strike!” Li Zhu’s sword abruptly flew from his hand and fell to the ground. Lu Junyi spurred his horse in pursuit, lightly stretched out his ape-like arm, twisted his wolf-like waist, and with one tug snatched Li Zhu alive across his saddle, then ordered the soldiers to bind him. Twisting his spear and urging on his horse, Lu Junyi charged in again to seek out Wang Qing, like a swift hawk pursuing a circling swallow or a fierce tiger devouring a lamb. The rebels threw away their gongs and abandoned their drums, cast aside halberds and dropped their spears; sons sought fathers, fathers sought sons, and brothers called for one another. Of more than a hundred thousand rebel soldiers, over half were slain. Corpses lay across the wilderness, and blood flowed in rivers. Thirty thousand surrendered. Apart from those who escaped, nearly all the rest were at death’s door, maimed and wounded, or sprawled upon the ground to be trampled by men and horses until flesh and bone became mud; their number was beyond counting. The two fierce generals Liu Yijing and Shangguan Yi had their warhorses cut down by Jiao Ting; when they tumbled from their saddles, he killed them both. Li Xiong was knocked from his horse by one of Qiongying’s flying stones and stabbed to death with a painted halberd. As Bi Xian was fleeing, Wang Dingliu, the “Living Flash,” suddenly sprang from concealment, knocked him from his horse with one thrust of his long-handled saber, then drove the blade into his chest and ended his life. The bogus ministers, privy councillors, palace commanders, imperial guards, generals, and all the rest failed to escape. Only the chief rebel Wang Qing had vanished. The Song army had won a great victory.

p.src: Song Jiang ordered the gongs sounded to recall and muster his troops, then advanced toward Nanfeng. He commanded Zhang Qing and Qiongying to lead five thousand cavalry ahead to reconnoiter; he also sent Dai Zong, the “Magic Messenger,” on ahead to learn how Sun An’s surprise attack on Nanfeng had fared. Dai Zong obeyed, invoked his magic-traveling art, and sped past Zhang Qing and Qiongying. After being gone only a short while, he returned and reported: “Acting on the vanguard commander’s orders, Sun An disguised his men as western troops in an attempt to trick his way into the city. But the rebels discovered the ruse, dug a pitfall inside the gate, then opened the eastern gate and allowed our troops and horses to enter. Seven of Sun An’s deputy generals—Mei Yu, Jin Zhen, Bi Jie, Pan Xun, Yang Fang, Feng Sheng, and Hu Mai—vied to be first into the city. They and five hundred soldiers, men and horses alike, all plunged into the pitfall. The ambushers on both sides sprang out together and, wielding long spears and sharp halberds, stabbed Mei Yu and the other five hundred men to death without exception. Fortunately, Sun An was in the rear. Seizing the moment, he fought bravely through the city gate and ordered his soldiers to fill the pitfall. Sun An rode foremost and led his troops into the city, and the rebels could not withstand them. Sun An seized the eastern gate, but the rebels then rallied from every side and hemmed in his troops there. When I learned this news, I flew back to report it. On the way I met General Zhang and Lady Zhang. When I told them what had happened, the two of them urged their forces into a swift gallop and hurried away.” On hearing the report, Song Jiang urged the main army swiftly forward and surrounded Nanfeng. By then Zhang Qing and Qiongying had entered through the eastern gate. They ordered Sun An to hold it while they fought fiercely against the rebel army. Thus Song Jiang and his commanders and troops rushed through the eastern gate, captured the city, scattered the rebels, and raised the Song army’s banners over all four gates. Fan Quan and the many bogus civil and military officials in the city were all put to death. When the bogus consort Duan Sanniang heard that the army had entered the city, she—being naturally strong and also a skilled rider—girded herself for battle and led more than a hundred sturdy palace attendants, all bearing weapons, out of the royal palace and through the rear garden. She intended to fight her way out of the western gate and flee to the Yun’an garrison, but there she met Qiongying leading troops into the rear garden. Lady Duan spurred her horse, leveled a precious saber, and charged with desperate fury. Qiongying sent a stone flying that struck Duan Sanniang squarely in the face. Blood spurted forth, and she crashed from her horse, tumbling heels over head; the soldiers rushed up, seized her, and bound her. All the palace attendants were killed by the Song troops. Qiongying led her troops through the rear garden into the inner palace. When the palace women and concubines heard that the Song army had entered the city, some hanged themselves, some threw themselves into wells, some cut their throats, and others dashed themselves against the steps. More than half took their own lives. Qiongying ordered her soldiers to bind all the survivors and escort them before Song Jiang’s command tent. Song Jiang was delighted. He had Lady Duan and her entire party imprisoned, intending to escort them all to the capital once Wang Qing had been captured. He then dispatched troops in every direction to pursue Wang Qing.

p.src: An attendant shouted, “You fishermen there! Pole a few boats over and ferry us across the river. We will pay you handsomely for the passage.” Two fishermen set down their wine bowls and rowed a little fishing skiff toward the bank, the oars creaking as it came. The fisherman at the bow took up a bamboo pole from beside the boat and punted it to shore. He scrutinized Wang Qing from head to foot, then said, “Excellent! Here comes something to buy us more wine. Come aboard, come aboard!” The attendant helped Wang Qing dismount. Wang Qing looked at the fisherman. He was tall and powerfully built, with thick eyebrows, large eyes, a ruddy face, whiskers like iron wire, and a voice like a bronze bell. Holding the bamboo pole in one hand, the fisherman helped Wang Qing aboard with the other. Then he merely planted the pole once against the bank, and the boat was already more than ten feet from shore. The bandit followers on shore fell into a panic and shouted together, “Bring the boat back at once! We have to cross the river too.” The fisherman glared at them and bellowed, “We are coming! What is your hurry?” Then he dropped the bamboo pole, seized Wang Qing by the front of his robe, and bore down with both hands, throwing him flat upon the deck with a thud. Wang Qing tried to struggle, but the man at the oar released it, sprang over, and helped pin him down. p.src: The man who had poled the boat was in fact Li Jun, the “River-Dragon,” while the oarsman was Tong Wei, the “Cave-Leaving Dragon.” Most of the other fishermen were naval troops. Under orders from the Song Vanguard, Li Jun had taken command of the naval vessels and come to engage the bandits' fleet. Li Jun and his men had fought a great battle against the bandit fleet in Qutang Gorge. They killed its commander-in-chief, the naval governor Wenren Shichong, captured his deputy Hu Jun, and utterly defeated the enemy forces. Seeing that Hu Jun was a man of uncommon bearing, Li Jun magnanimously released him; grateful for this mercy, Hu Jun joined Li Jun in tricking the defenders into opening Yun'an's water gate. They captured the city and killed the false governor Shi Jun and his associates. Li Jun, the “River-Dragon,” had reckoned that if the bandits were defeated in battle with the imperial army, they would be certain to flee back toward their lairs. He had therefore ordered Zhang Heng and Zhang Shun to defend the city, while he himself took Tong Wei and Tong Meng with a force of naval troops, disguised their craft as fishing boats, and patrolled this place on reconnaissance; he had also ordered the three Ruan brothers to disguise themselves as fishermen and split up to lie in ambush and scout the various routes by Yanyu Reef, the Min River, and Yufu Inlet. A moment earlier Li Jun had seen Wang Qing riding foremost with many men clustered behind him. He guessed that the man must be a bandit chieftain, though he did not know that this was the arch-rebel himself. Li Jun now questioned the attendants and, learning that the captive was Wang Qing, clapped his hands and laughed aloud. He had the prisoners bound and taken into Yun'an. He sent men to recall the three Ruan brothers, while the two Zhangs remained to defend the city. Then Li Jun and the surrendered general Hu Jun escorted Wang Qing and his entire party to the Song Vanguard's army. On the way they learned that Song Jiang had already taken Nanfeng, so Li Jun and the others proceeded straight into the city and delivered Wang Qing to the commander's residence. Song Jiang had been troubled because his generals had failed to track down Wang Qing, and he was overjoyed when the report arrived. Li Jun entered the residence and paid his respects to the Song Vanguard. Song Jiang praised him, saying, “Worthy brother, this is no small achievement.” Li Jun brought the surrendered general Hu Jun forward to pay his respects to the Song Vanguard. Li Jun said, “The credit belongs entirely to this man.” Song Jiang asked Hu Jun his name and questioned him about how Yun'an had been taken by stratagem.
